config.helpPageGettingStartedBody:
The first time you open nextDash, a quick-start card in the corner walks through four short steps: language and auto dark mode, how the grid is laid out, whether to show the weather, and your starting point. Skip it whenever you like — nothing is locked in, and every setting it touches stays reachable under Config → General. After the steps it becomes a small checklist: add a bookmark, open config, and look at the keyboard shortcuts. Finish or dismiss it and it does not come back.

Once you're in, the essentials fit in half a minute:

  • > search — type part of a name, Enter opens the top result
  • + or Shift+B full new-bookmark form  ·  & one-line quick add on the dashboard (name | url | shortcut)
  • 0 Inbox  ·  * recent bookmarks  ·  ! or F1 keyboard cheat sheet
  • Ctrl+K quick actions  ·  Ctrl+Shift+K find any setting or help section

Most layout and behaviour lives under Config → General, and the ℹ button next to almost every setting explains what it does without leaving the form. After a new release you may see a one-time What's new summary; you can reopen it any time from Advanced → System → Onboarding & tips, which is also where you bring the quick-start card back. Now and then the dashboard also shows a single keyboard tip as a small toast, with a Cheat sheet button beside it. The tips come from the Tips & tricks section below, appear at most once every few days, never repeat one you have already seen, and stay away during first-run setup and while a dialog or the inline editor is open. Switch them off with Show occasional keyboard tips in the same Onboarding & tips section.

On a brand-new install the quick-start card ends with a Starting point step: keep the example bookmarks to explore a ready-made dashboard, or choose Start from scratch for a completely empty one. If you ever end up with no bookmarks at all, the dashboard shows a friendly empty state with a button to add your first one and links into config — pressing + opens the full add-bookmark form.
config.helpPageConfiguringBody:
Settings are grouped into tabs — System (General, Theme, Backups, Stats, Keyboard), Dashboard (Pages, Categories, Bookmarks), Extras (Tags, Finders, Collections), and Help — with the active group highlighted and a dot on any group with unsaved changes (e.g. System ●). A breadcrumb under the tabs shows where you are (General › Layout), and the save row tells you whether the current tab needs an explicit Save or saves automatically (Collections and Finders save on their own). On a phone the tab bar collapses to a simpler set.

General is the control room for the whole dashboard, and its toolbar switches between three layers. Essentials covers Localization (language, date, time, weather), Appearance (theme, fonts, animations), Layout (Classic/Modern, density, columns, title), Bookmarks (display and behaviour), Smart Collections (which automatic groups are on), and Header & buttons (which footer and corner buttons show). Advanced adds finer tuning for the same areas plus a few that only live here: background images and fonts, Smart Collections limits, Diagnostics & status (health pings), Branding & identity (title, favicon), Search & input behaviour, and System & tools (reset buttons and What's new). All sections puts everything on one scrollable page for a full overview.

Like this Help tab and Stats, General has a sticky quick links sidebar next to the settings — opening a section from the sidebar or by clicking its title collapses whichever other section was open, so only one stays expanded at a time; on narrow screens the sidebar becomes a horizontal chip bar instead. Changes do not apply until you press Save, after which the dashboard refreshes in place without a full reload.
config.helpPageKeyboardBody: Dashboard shortcuts use fixed defaults — open the cheat sheet with ! or F1 for a searchable list (also under Config → Help → Keyboard). With a bookmark row selected, Shift+M moves it, Shift+T opens quick-tag, and Shift+D deletes with undo in the toast. Home, End, and Page Up/Page Down jump larger distances through the grid — see Navigation above for page-level keys.
config.helpPageSearchToolbarBody:
Search is really three modes behind one overlay, switchable by typing a prefix or clicking a tab at the top: > for normal search, : for commands, and ? for finders. A lone : opens grouped commands (bookmarks, navigation, layout, smart collections, settings) with recent commands floating to the top — try :layout modern, :density compact, :sort, :backup, :export, :inbox, or :quicktag to see how much of config has a matching command. Filters such as tag:work, category:news, status:online, and page:2 narrow normal-search results without touching the dashboard layout, and combine freely with plain text.

The dashboard footer holds a row of buttons for the actions you reach for most: + bookmark opens the full new-bookmark form, search opens the overlay in search mode, commands opens it in command mode, finders opens it in finder mode, recent lists your last-opened bookmarks, and the cheat sheet shows every shortcut with its own search box. Two more floating buttons appear in the corners when enabled: the tag cloud FAB (/) opens a popularity-scaled word cloud for multi-tag filtering, and the What's new star opens a short changelog the first time a release ships, or any time from here via Show what's new above. Which of these buttons are visible is configurable under General → Header & buttons — hide the ones you never use to keep the footer minimal.

Two different shortcuts are easy to confuse: Ctrl+K (Cmd+K on Mac) runs quick actions only — save, jump to the dashboard — while Ctrl+Shift+K searches every setting and help section across all of config and expands the matching panel automatically.
config.helpPageOrganizingBody:
On the dashboard, bookmarks behave like a small spreadsheet: arrow keys move the selection, ; opens inline edit on the highlighted row, and a long press opens the same editor with touch. A plain click opens the bookmark itself, while dragging a row — from anywhere on it — reorders the bookmark within its category or drops it into another one; a drag never opens the editor, and a click never reorders. Grid navigation pauses while inline edit is open so you cannot accidentally jump away, and edits to smart-collection rows update the real bookmark everywhere it appears. Right-click a bookmark for its actions in one menu: open in a new tab, copy the URL, edit, tags, move, or delete. Everything there is also reachable from the command palette or config — the menu just puts it where most people look first. Arrow keys and Enter work inside it, deleting still asks for confirmation, and Shift + right-click gives you the browser's own menu.

Pinned bookmarks always float to the top of their category and sort alphabetically among themselves; everyone else follows the category's sort mode — manual drag, A–Z, or Recent, switched via the chips in each category header. While a category is on A–Z or Recent its bookmarks can't be dragged to reorder — a hover tooltip, a not-allowed cursor, and a brief note explain to switch it back to manual order first. Bookmarks without a category land in an Other bucket at the end of the page. Long-press a category header to rename it, or drag the // prefix in its title to reorder categories; the same order can be edited in Config → Categories. Press . anywhere on the dashboard to collapse or expand every category at once. Command mode :sort applies to the focused category if you prefer the keyboard.

There are several ways to add a bookmark: + opens the full form, & adds one in a single line on the dashboard (name | url | shortcut), pasting a URL (Ctrl+V) offers a quick prompt, and the browser extension saves the current tab. The full form's Page and Category dropdowns each carry a + New… option, so you can create a page or category inline and save it straight away without first adding a bookmark. Every bookmark can carry a shortcut letter, tags, a note, a custom icon, and an optional status check that pings the URL to show online/offline state right on its row.
config.helpPageWorkspaceBody:
Config → Pages creates, renames, reorders (drag or the ↑/↓ buttons, auto-saved), and archives pages. Archiving hides a page from the header tabs without deleting its bookmarks, so nothing is lost if you bring it back later.

On the dashboard you can also customise a page tab in place: double-click the tab (desktop and tablet landscape — not on mobile, to avoid accidental edits on touch) to open a small popover where you rename the page, set an optional emoji, and pick a colour dot from eight swatches. The dot appears on the tab beside the label so you can tell pages apart at a glance; choose the empty swatch to remove it. Changes save when you click away or press Enter. Use Config → Pages when you need to rename on a phone or edit several pages in a list.

Config → Categories works the same way, plus merging: drag one category's bookmarks into another to combine them and remove the empty one. The order set here matches the dashboard exactly, and can also be changed by dragging the // prefix in a category's title on the dashboard.

Config → Bookmarks is built for bulk work: a filterable, sortable list on the left, a detail editor on the right, and a collapsible Context panel to switch page and category without losing your place in the list. Select multiple rows to move, pin, tag (add, replace, or remove), delete, or refresh favicons together, and conflict highlighting flags duplicate URLs or shortcuts before you save. Ctrl+Shift+K jumps to any setting from here, and Ctrl+K runs quick actions. To refresh every icon at once instead of a selection, run :favicons fetch on the dashboard: it re-downloads the favicon of every bookmark on every page, replacing the ones already stored. On a new install this runs once by itself after you finish or skip the setup card with the example bookmarks kept.
config.helpPageTagsCollectionsBody:
Tags are free-form labels added in config or inline on the dashboard, normalised on save (trimmed, lowercased, deduplicated) and suggested by autocomplete as you type an existing one. In search, tag:work filters results without rearranging the grid; on desktop, the tag cloud (/ or its corner button) colour-codes tags by how often they're used and lets you toggle several at once while the modal stays open, matching bookmarks with any selected tag (OR logic) — a clear button resets the filter in one click. Command mode :tag work lists matches in the palette only, without changing the dashboard.

Smart collections are automatic groups — Today, Recently opened, Stale bookmarks (not opened in a while), and Most used (ranked by open count) — each toggled per page with an optional item limit (0 = unlimited); a master switch under Essentials turns them all on or off at once, with per-page detail under Advanced. They sit alongside ordinary categories and collapse the same way. Turning on Tag collections under General → Smart Collections spawns one dynamic group per heavily-used tag, with a minimum bookmark count so rare tags do not clutter the dashboard.

Custom collections (Config → Collections) are rule-based instead: give one a name, an optional emoji, AND/OR match logic, and rules on tag, category, or shortcut. Each rule's value field autocompletes from the tags, categories, and shortcuts already in use, so you rarely have to type a full value. An AND collection with category:work and tag:urgent surfaces only bookmarks matching both; an OR collection with tag:reading and tag:later catches either. Matching bookmarks appear as read-only dashboard sections, sorted before ordinary categories, and save immediately with no separate Save button.
config.helpPageInboxBody:
Inbox is a lightweight capture list for links to read or sort later, separate from bookmark pages. Open it from the Inbox tab in the header, press 0 on the dashboard (search closed), or run :inbox.

Paste a URL on the dashboard (Ctrl+V) and choose Save to Inbox or Add bookmark — or set a default under General → Paste URL default (Ask every time, Always bookmark, or Always Inbox) to skip the prompt entirely. The browser extension can also save to Inbox, and duplicate URLs are rejected with a toast.

On the Inbox page, filter All/Unread, search, and browse by date group (Today, Yesterday, This week, Older). Each item can be opened, Promoted to a full bookmark (pre-fills the new-bookmark form with page and category to pick), or deleted with undo. New items stay unread until opened or triaged; a tab badge shows the unread count.

Triage walks items one by one, keyboard-only:

  • J/K move  ·  O/Enter open
  • P promote to a full bookmark  ·  R/Space keep (marks read)
  • D/Delete remove  ·  Esc close triage

Start it from the Triage button or :inbox triage. Toggle the tab itself under General → Enable Inbox page.

Sorting, links and selections. Next to the search box, sort by newest first (the default), oldest first, title, or site. Oldest-first is how a backlog actually gets worked — the items you have been avoiding are at the bottom — and sorting by title or site drops the date headings so the ordering runs unbroken. Filter, sort and search all appear in the address bar, so a view can be bookmarked or shared, and filter and sort come back on your next visit; a shared link wins over that, and the search box is deliberately not remembered. Tick rows with their checkbox or x to act on just those: Mark read, Snooze or Delete, rather than the toolbar's all-or-nothing bulk. Esc clears the selection, changing filter clears it too so nothing hidden can be caught up in a bulk action, and a bulk delete names the count before it runs. Snooze offers four presets plus a date of your own for anything further out than next week.
config.helpPageHealthStatusBody:
Status monitoring optionally pings bookmarks to show online/offline state right on their dashboard row. Enable it under General → Advanced → Status, choose whether to show ping detail and a loading spinner, and use Skip fast ping check if background noise is too high — useful on flaky networks or when you have many bookmarks.

For deeper triage, open the dashboard Health view (/#health). Summary cards total healthy, broken, duplicate, stale, and unchecked bookmarks; click one to filter the list, and search, status filters, sorting, and retest actions sit in one compact toolbar. Each row shows a 0–100 health score that factors in whether a bookmark has ever been opened, how stale it is, and whether its URL or shortcut conflicts with another bookmark, alongside repair actions: re-check status, detect redirect, refresh title, refresh favicon, or archive. Merging two duplicates keeps one row and folds the other's tags and notes into it.

Click any score badge — or press s — to see how it was reached: every bookmark starts at 100 and each issue shows what it costs. A repaired bookmark turns green straight away, and an applied redirect is checked against the new address before the row counts as healthy. Note that Retest statuses only checks bookmarks that have Check status switched on (off by default, set per bookmark in Config → Bookmarks) plus anything already flagged with an error; it says so when there is nothing to test.

The page is built for the keyboard: j/k or arrows move focus, Tab steps one row at a time, g/G jump to first/last, Enter opens the bookmark in config and o opens the URL. On the focused row, s shows the score breakdown, p re-checks, f refreshes the favicon, x selects, m opens more actions and c changes availability checking. The legend at the top of the page lists them all. The page follows your dashboard's layout and theme, so it feels like part of the same app rather than a separate tool.

Availability checking is one choice of three. A bookmark is either Off (never tested), Periodic (checked about once a day, and flagged when it breaks), or Monitor (checked on its own interval — 5 minutes to 24 hours — keeping 30 days of history). Monitor does everything Periodic does, so there is never a reason to want both. Change it from the mode button on any health row (or press c), from the bookmark right-click menu on the dashboard, with Shift+C on the selected bookmark, or in the bookmark editor; each option carries its own letter, o, p and m. When the list is filtered, a bulk button offers to switch just those rows at once and names the exact count first — it is deliberately never offered on the unfiltered All list.

Monitored bookmarks keep a history. Their rows add a heartbeat bar of recent checks, an uptime percentage over 24 hours, 7 days and 30 days, and a response-time sparkline; opening a row shows its outage history — when each one started, how long it lasted and what went wrong — or down since while it is still down. A Monitored filter narrows the list to these rows. Set an alert webhook under General → Status monitoring and nextDash posts when a monitored bookmark goes down and again when it recovers, waiting for three failed checks in a row by default so a single hiccup stays quiet. Local addresses are refused unless Allow local bookmarks is on.

Open a monitored bookmark's statistics at full size. The row itself only has room for a 24-hour figure and one response time, so the ⤢ button at the end of its monitor strip — or i on the selected row — opens the rest: a large response-time chart with the minimum, average and maximum marked and a tooltip on every point, uptime for 24 hours, 7 days and 30 days side by side with the number of checks behind each, a taller heartbeat bar, the check interval and last check, and the full outage list. It opens instantly because it shows the report already on screen rather than fetching anything new, so it can never disagree with the row underneath it. A window with no samples yet reads no data instead of 0%, so a monitor you enabled an hour ago is not mistaken for a day of downtime. Esc closes it and leaves your place in the list. The button only appears once there is something to show — a monitored bookmark still waiting for its first check does not get one.

Reading a value off the chart. The chart is interactive rather than decorative. Click or hover anywhere in a measurement's slice of the plot — a full-height column, not just the dot — and the readout under the chart names it: the response time, the time it was measured, how many checks that point folds together, and whether it was up, down or degraded. It opens on the most recent measurement rather than empty. ← and → walk from point to point and update the readout as they go, stepping over buckets with no measurement so you never land on an empty reading. The whole chart is a single Tab stop, so Close stays one Tab away instead of one per measurement.

Take the list with you. Export downloads whatever the filter and search currently show as CSV — name, URL, status, score, page, category, last checked, and the same issue wording the score panel gives — for working through findings beside a spreadsheet or handing someone the list. Your filter and sort are remembered for the next visit, though a shared ?hv_filter= link still wins. The Monitored filter is now offered as soon as you have bookmarks rather than only once something is already monitored, and an empty Monitored list explains what monitoring does instead of reporting that nothing is wrong.
config.helpPageAppearanceBody:
Pick a look under Essentials → Layout: Classic (dense, list-first), or Modern (card-based with more breathing room) — same underlying structure, different polish, and Modern is early-beta. Density has four levels — Compact, Comfortable, Dense, and Auto (adapts to screen and zoom) — and column count and dashboard title live in the same panel. Switch layout version from the dashboard with :layoutversion to try one before saving.

Advanced → Appearance adds background images or presets, a UI font (including an uploaded custom font file), and favicon harmonisation, which recolours mismatched site favicons so they don't clash with your theme. New installs start with it switched on; it is configured per theme, so the dark and light variant of a pair are set separately. Auto dark mode follows the system theme. Random theme sits under Config → Appearance → Theme, below your saved theme choice: Off always uses the theme above; On page refresh draws a new built-in theme on every reload (F5); On view change picks again when you switch between bookmarks, config, inbox, and health, or when you switch dashboard pages (tabs, 1–9, swipe, or hash). While random is on, a Currently showing line names the theme on screen. With auto dark mode enabled, only dark or light variants matching your system appearance are eligible — custom single-palette themes are skipped. Theme colours live on their own Theme tab with live preview, packaged palettes, JSON import/export, and undo; a shortcut link elsewhere in config opens it directly.

The header's date/time/weather line is optional and configured under General: toggle date and time independently, with formats from compact numeric to long weekday names, and 24- or 12-hour clocks. With weather enabled, choose browser geolocation or a manual city, Celsius or Fahrenheit, and a refresh interval.

On narrow screens, portrait tablets, or touch devices, nextDash switches to a lighter chrome — the dashboard footer keeps just Search and + Bookmark, with commands and finders folded into the search overlay's >/:/? tabs. The cheat sheet and some footer buttons are desktop-only, and config on a phone focuses on the settings you're most likely to need on the go — the full split-view bookmark editor expects a wider window.

Items per category. A category shows only its first 15 bookmarks by default, with the rest behind a + N more / show less toggle so one long category cannot tower over the others. Change the limit or switch it off under Config → General → Layout; smart collections are never capped, and an expanded category stays expanded. The toggle is reachable from the keyboard too: arrow onto it and press Enter.
config.helpPageDataBackupsBody:
Server data lives in ./data by default — override with NEXTDASH_DATA_DIR for Docker volumes or multiple instances. Open dashboard tabs poll a revision endpoint so bookmark grids refresh when another tab saves changes, and link preview metadata is cached on the server and flushed periodically. When enabled, device-specific settings are stored in the browser's local storage, so one computer can keep different visual preferences than another.

Config → Backups handles the rest. A ZIP export includes pages, bookmarks, categories, finders, your inbox, settings, themes, and the uptime history of monitored bookmarks — import replaces everything, so export first (:backup opens the tab, :export downloads immediately). The write token and other environment variables are not part of the ZIP; they live in your server's environment, not in exported data.

Automatic backups keep a safety net on the server: once a week nextDash writes a full ZIP under data/auto-backups/ and keeps the latest 3, removing the oldest as new ones are made. The Automatic Backups section lists each one with its date and size, with Download, Restore (roll back to that backup in one click), and Delete buttons, a Back Up Now button, and a countdown to the next run. It's on by default and can be turned off with a single toggle. Keep data/ on a mounted volume so these survive container rebuilds.

You can also import a browser's HTML bookmark export (folders become categories, duplicates are skipped, with a preview before you commit) or export everything to CSV — name, URL, page, category, shortcut, tags, and notes — for spreadsheets or a quick audit outside nextDash.

Under Config → General → Reset there are two destructive buttons. The red Reset all data wipes everything and starts over from the default sample dashboard. The amber Delete all bookmarks only empties every page's bookmarks but keeps your pages, categories, finders and settings — and does not put the sample bookmarks back. Both ask for confirmation and then for you to type a word, so neither can happen by accident.

Monitoring history is the one piece of health data that is archived, because it is measured rather than derived: without it a restore leaves every monitored bookmark waiting for its first check, with no chart, no uptime windows and no outage list, and a 30-day figure takes 30 days to earn back. The preview and health caches are deliberately left out and cleared on import — a scan rebuilds those in minutes. A ZIP written before this was added simply has no history in it; restoring one leaves whatever history you already have in place rather than wiping it.
config.helpPageFindersBody:
Finders are search shortcuts that send a query to an external site — for example ?g your terms for Google. Define them under Config → Finders with a shortcut letter and a URL containing %s where the query belongs. Reorder with drag or arrow keys; duplicates are flagged before save.

When Include finders in search is on, a bookmark and a finder with the same shortcut both appear in results. A guided tour on first visit can add a sample Google finder; replay it from System & tools anytime.
config.helpPageSelfHostingBody:
The browser extension (in extension/) saves the current tab to nextDash. Install it unpacked in Chrome, set the server URL, and paste the write token if your server uses NEXTDASH_WRITE_TOKEN. The save form supports an optional shortcut (auto-suggested from the title), tags, and notes, warns about duplicate URLs, and can Save to Inbox instead of picking a page. If CORS is restricted, add your chrome-extension:// origin to NEXTDASH_CORS_ORIGINS.

nextDash has no built-in user accounts — anyone who can reach the URL can read and write data unless you protect it with a VPN, private network, or reverse-proxy authentication. Do not expose plain HTTP to the public internet. Set NEXTDASH_WRITE_TOKEN so write APIs require the X-NextDash-Token header (the dashboard and config pages inject it automatically once you're signed in via the browser), restrict NEXTDASH_CORS_ORIGINS for the extension, and tune activity logging with NEXTDASH_ACTIVITY_LOG (mutate, status, open, security, or off) — outbound fetches already validate public IPs to reduce SSRF risk. Docker Compose is the recommended way to run nextDash long-term; docker-compose.prod.yml mounts only ./data and serves assets from the embedded binary (since v2026.08.02 ~40% smaller, non-root, optional Caddy proxy for TLS).

If bookmarks seem to vanish, check the page and category filters in config first — it's usually a filter, not data loss. Sorting surprises usually mean a category is in A–Z or Recent mode, or a pin is doing its job; search gaps often clear up with fuzzy mode or filters like tag:work. Extension save failures almost always trace back to the server URL, write token, or CORS; API 401 means a missing token, 429 means you hit a rate limit — outbound and API rate limits exist to protect the server, and settle down within a minute or two.

Privacy-friendly analytics. nextDash can record anonymous usage statistics through a self-hosted Umami instance, so it is visible which features are actually used and where the app can be improved. It is never about following you personally: no bookmark names, URLs, search queries, page names, notes or tags are sent, no cookies are set, and there is no tracking across other sites — purely abstract, technical measurement of flow and feature usage, aggregated across everyone. It is off unless you turn it on: Config → General → Advanced → Privacy, or run :telemetry on from the command palette. While it is off, the tracker script is not emitted at all, so it is never downloaded and no request leaves your machine. If you host nextDash for other people, set the environment variable DISABLE_TELEMETRY=true to switch analytics off for the whole server: it can then not be re-enabled from the app, and the Privacy checkbox appears greyed out with a note explaining why. With that variable set, :telemetry lists a single row saying it is off for this server instead of offering a choice it cannot honour.
config.helpPageTipsBody: Small things that make nextDash faster. Use the filter above to search them.
config.tipConfigKeyboard: In config: j/k move sections or the bookmark list, 0–9 leave for Inbox or a page, and Ctrl+Shift+K finds any setting — press ! for the full cheat sheet. Shift+S returns where you left off.
config.tipEverydayModes: Type > to search, : for commands, ? for finders — all from the keyboard, no clicking.
config.tipEverydayPages: 1–9 jumps straight to a page; Shift+←/→ steps through them.
config.tipEverydayArrows: ↑↓←→ moves between bookmarks, Enter opens the selected one.
config.tipEverydayEsc: Esc always backs out of whatever is open.
config.tipEverydayOverview: , shows every page with its bookmark count.
config.tipEverydayViews: Shift+H opens health, Shift+I the inbox, and Shift+S config — the header icons use the same keys.
config.tipEverydayCheatsheet: ! or F1 opens the full keyboard cheat sheet — every shortcut in one place.
config.tipAddPaste: Paste a URL anywhere on the dashboard and the new-bookmark modal opens pre-filled.
config.tipAddQuickAdd: & is the fastest way in: type name | url | shortcut in one field.
config.tipAddFullModal: + or Shift+B opens the full modal when you need page, category, tags and preview.
config.tipAddShortcut: Give a bookmark a shortcut and you can open it later by just typing that shortcut.
config.tipEditInline: ; edits the selected bookmark inline — no dialog, no page change.
config.tipEditQuickActions: Shift+M moves it, Shift+T tags it, Shift+D deletes it. Each opens a small popover.
config.tipEditUndo: Deleted the wrong one? The toast has an Undo for a few seconds.
config.tipEditDrag: Drag the strip on the left of a row to reorder; drag the // in a category header to reorder categories.
config.tipEditRenamePage: Double-click a page tab to rename it and give it an emoji and colour.
config.tipEditPageTabDot: Double-click a page tab and pick a colour swatch — a colour dot appears on the tab so you can tell pages apart at a glance.
config.tipFindFilters: Search narrows with tag:, category:, status: and page: — combine them with plain words.
config.tipFindAllPages: Prefix a search with @ to look across every page instead of the current one.
config.tipFindFinders: Finders send your text to a search engine: ?g term googles it.
config.tipFindTagCloud: / opens the tag cloud — click a tag to filter the dashboard down to it.
config.tipFindRecent: * lists what you opened recently; :open last 5 reopens them in tabs.
config.tipMaintHealth: The health page finds broken links, duplicates and bookmarks you have not touched in a long time.
config.tipMaintMerge: Duplicates can be merged from the health page in one bulk action.
config.tipMaintMonitorStats: Press i on a monitored bookmark in the health view to open its full statistics — uptime over 24 hours, 7 days and 30 days, a large response-time chart and every outage.
config.tipMaintCert: A certificate about to expire is invisible until it breaks. Monitored bookmarks on HTTPS warn you 30, 7 and 3 days ahead — the health view badges the rows and counts them in a Certificates tile.
config.tipMaintExpectText: A page can answer perfectly while showing “Database connection failed”. On a monitored row, set Expected response to a phrase that only appears when it works, and a broken page stops counting as up.
config.tipMaintMaintenanceWindow: Alerted every night by a backup that takes a host down for ten minutes? A maintenance window under Behavior → Status & health silences the expected downtime without hiding a real outage.
config.tipMaintTrash: Deleted something you wanted? Deleted bookmarks, pages and categories wait 30 days in config → data & backups → trash, long after the undo toast has gone.
config.tipMaintBackup: Back up everything — pages, bookmarks and settings — under config → data & backups. Restoring replaces what you have, so back up first.
config.tipMaintNote: :note edits a bookmark's note without leaving the dashboard.
config.tipTuneInfo: Every setting in config has an ℹ button explaining what it does.
config.tipTuneTheme: The dark/light button in the header flips the theme instantly, without touching config.
config.tipTunePreview: Link preview cards are off by default — turn them on under config → appearance → display, then hover a bookmark.
config.tipTuneSmartCollections: Smart collections fill themselves from rules; you never add bookmarks to them by hand.
config.tipTuneCommands: Commands like :favicons off or :dark change settings live, without a round trip to config.

config.statusBrowserChecksNote: How the dashboard tests the bookmarks on screen while you have it open. Applies to bookmarks set to Periodic or Monitor; a bookmark set to Off is never tested.
config.statusServerChecksNote: Re-tests bookmarks on the server, so the Health view stays current without anyone having the dashboard open. Off by default because it makes outbound requests.
config.statusAlertsNote: Posts to a webhook when a monitored bookmark goes down and again when it recovers. Only monitored bookmarks raise alerts — Periodic flags a broken link in the Health view but never notifies.
config.statsNoActivity: No bookmarks were used in this period.
config.statsNeverOpenedHint: Candidates to tidy up — they have never been used.
config.statsAllOpened: Everything has been opened at least once.
config.statsScoreHint: Starts at 100 and loses points for bookmarks you never open, links gone stale, duplicate URLs and clashing shortcuts.
config.overviewNothingToDo: Nothing needs attention — everything checks out.

config.overviewNewFeatureSpacingTitle: Decide how much room the grid gives away
config.overviewNewFeatureSpacingWhat: The gap between category rows and the empty band down both edges were both fixed, and on a wide screen they added up to a lot of nothing.
config.overviewNewFeatureSpacingHow: Config → Appearance → Layout now has Category spacing and Page margins, each with Snug, Balanced and Airy.
config.overviewNewFeatureSpacingEnable: Page margins start exactly where they always were. Category spacing is a little tighter than before — pick Airy for the old gap.
config.overviewNewFeatureStructureTrashTitle: Deleted pages and categories come back
config.overviewNewFeatureStructureTrashWhat: Deleting a page took its bookmarks with it and kept nothing anywhere, so the more one click destroyed, the less you could recover.
config.overviewNewFeatureStructureTrashHow: Both now go to the trash for 30 days. A page is one entry — listed as “Page · 12 bookmarks” — and restoring brings the page, its categories and its bookmarks back in a single action.
config.overviewNewFeatureStructureTrashEnable: Nothing to switch on. The delete toast also offers Undo for eight seconds, and a page returns to its original slot rather than as a copy nothing points at.
config.overviewNewFeatureCategoryGridTitle: Add a category from the grid itself
config.overviewNewFeatureCategoryGridWhat: Making a category meant going into Config or through the bookmark form — both things you did on the way to something else.
config.overviewNewFeatureCategoryGridHow: A + sits beside the A–Z / Rec chips in a category header, and holding c does the same from the keyboard. Both act on the page on screen, so neither asks which page you meant.
config.overviewNewFeatureCategoryGridEnable: Nothing to switch on. Right-click a category header to rename or delete it, and a category you just made stays visible even with “hide empty categories” on.
config.overviewNewFeaturePageOverviewTitle: Make a page from the pages overview
config.overviewNewFeaturePageOverviewWhat: Adding a page lived in Config, away from the list of pages you were already looking at.
config.overviewNewFeaturePageOverviewHow: Press , for the overview and use the New page row under the list — by click, by n, or by arrowing one stop past the last page.
config.overviewNewFeaturePageOverviewEnable: Nothing to switch on. Creating takes you straight to the new page, which is where its first category gets added anyway.
config.overviewNewFeatureHealthBulkTitle: Fix a whole list of broken links at once
config.overviewNewFeatureHealthBulkWhat: Health lists exactly what a clear-out starts from — broken, duplicate, stale — and then made you repair them one row at a time.
config.overviewNewFeatureHealthBulkHow: Tick the box on any row, or press x to tick the one under the cursor and move on, X for everything the filter shows. A bar appears above the list with Set checking, Re-check, Open, Copy links and Delete.
config.overviewNewFeatureHealthBulkEnable: Nothing to switch on. Deletes go to the trash, and a row that changed since the report was built is skipped rather than deleted.
config.overviewNewFeatureBulkTagsWhat: Tagging worked one bookmark at a time, so putting the same tag on eight rows meant eight rounds.
config.overviewNewFeatureBulkTagsHow: Select some rows and press the toolbar’s Tags button. Every tag you already use is listed, with a tick when the whole selection has it and “on 2 of 3” when only some do.
config.overviewNewFeatureBulkTagsEnable: Nothing to switch on. Clicking a tag the whole selection already has takes it off instead; setting a category lives in the Move button beside it.
config.overviewNewFeatureFormCreateTitle: Make a page or category while adding a bookmark
config.overviewNewFeatureFormCreateWhat: Filing a bookmark somewhere that did not exist yet meant leaving the half-filled form, making the page or category in Config, and starting over.
config.overviewNewFeatureFormCreateHow: Both dropdowns in the bookmark form lead with ➕ New page… and ➕ New category…. Picking one swaps the dropdown for a name box, and the new page or category is selected when you come back.
config.overviewNewFeatureFormCreateEnable: Nothing to switch on. A category is made on whichever page the form is pointing at, including one you created moments earlier.
config.overviewNewFeatureMultiSelectTitle: Select several bookmarks with x and X
config.overviewNewFeatureMultiSelectWhat: Bulk move and bulk delete used to live in the tag filter, so acting on several bookmarks meant they had to share a tag. Any rows will do now — x ticks one, X takes a whole category.
config.overviewNewFeatureMultiSelectHow: Press x to tick the row under the cursor, X for the whole category, Shift+↑/↓ for a range, Ctrl/Cmd+A for everything on screen — or Ctrl+click and Shift+click with the mouse. Select is in the right-click menu too.
config.overviewNewFeatureMultiSelectEnable: Nothing to switch on. A toolbar appears with Move, Open, Copy links and Delete; Escape clears the selection.
config.overviewNewFeatureTrashWhat: Deleting a bookmark used to be final. It now goes to a trash and stays there for 30 days before going for good.
config.overviewNewFeatureTrashHow: Restore puts a bookmark back on its own page at its old position. Delete forever and Empty trash clear it early.
config.overviewNewFeatureTrashEnable: On by default, and it covers every delete — including a bulk delete of twenty rows at once. Under Config → Data & backups → Trash.
config.overviewNewFeatureHealthContextMenuWhat: The nine actions behind a health row’s More button were reachable only by hovering the row and finding the button.
config.overviewNewFeatureHealthContextMenuHow: Right-click any row in the Health view to open that same menu at the cursor, the way a bookmark on the dashboard already did. Shift and right-click still gives you the browser’s own menu.
config.overviewNewFeatureHealthContextMenuEnabl: Nothing to switch on — it is simply there. The ⋯ button and the m key keep working as before.
config.overviewNewFeatureMonitorEmphasisWhat: A bookmark set to Monitor now shows its status on the dashboard, the way a Periodic one always did — and you can say how much it should stand out.
config.overviewNewFeatureMonitorEmphasisHow: Right-click a bookmark and pick Show in Health to jump straight to its row, from the dashboard or from Config → Bookmarks.
config.overviewNewFeatureMonitorEmphasisEnable: Set to draw the eye only when something is down. Choose Always or Never under Config → Behavior → Status & health.
config.overviewNewFeatureSideRailWhat: The add, search, commands, and finders buttons can float center-bottom, dock into either bottom corner, or stand as a vertical rail down the left edge.
config.overviewNewFeatureSideRailHow: Pick a position under Config → Appearance → Layout, or run :buttonbar from the command palette. The bar moves as you choose — no reload.
config.overviewNewFeatureSideRailEnable: The side rail keeps the space under your bookmarks clear, which pays off on wide screens.
config.overviewNewFeatureBookmarkFormWhat: Add and edit bookmarks in one centered modal — from the dashboard, Health, Inbox, Config, and search.
config.overviewNewFeatureBookmarkFormHow: Press +, Shift+B, or Ctrl+Shift+A to open the form. Use Create + New to save and immediately add another; the grid updates behind the modal.
config.overviewNewFeatureBookmarkFormEnable: Press ! for the full cheat sheet. Edit a row with ; or from Health and Inbox action bars.
config.overviewNewFeatureUpdateCheckWhat: nextDash can compare your running version with GitHub once a day — a dot on ★, a toast while you are actively using the app, and a manual check in the ★ modal and Config → Overview.
config.overviewNewFeatureUpdateCheckHow: Press Check for updates in the ★ modal header or on Config → Overview. When a newer release exists, open GitHub from the notice or dismiss it until the next version.
config.overviewNewFeatureUpdateCheckEnable: On by default under Config → Behavior → Privacy. Turn off Check GitHub for new releases if you prefer no outbound request.
config.overviewNewFeatureBookmarksFiltersWhat: Search, filter, and sort the full bookmark library from one list — with chips that show what is active and summary tiles that follow your filters.
config.overviewNewFeatureBookmarksFiltersHow: Type in the search box (shortcuts match too), pick page or category from the dropdowns, or click a page, category, or tag on a row. Sort by last opened, most opened, or pinned first. Tick rows for bulk favicon refresh or CSV export.
config.overviewNewFeatureBookmarksFiltersEnable: Open Config → Bookmarks. Scroll to load more rows; press o or double-click a row to open its URL.
config.overviewNewFeaturePagesTagsTabsWhat: Pages & tags now opens on Categories, with Tags right beside it — the two lists you reach for most often.
config.overviewNewFeaturePagesTagsTabsHow: Use [ and ] to cycle sub-tabs from anywhere in config, or click Categories or Tags in the strip. Pages, Finders, and Collections follow after.
config.overviewNewFeaturePagesTagsTabsEnable: Open Config → Pages & tags — Categories is selected by default.
config.overviewNewFeatureRandomThemeWhat: Let nextDash pick a different built-in theme from the pool instead of always showing your saved choice. Your saved theme remains the default whenever random is off.
config.overviewNewFeatureRandomThemeHow: Choose Off (always your saved theme), On page refresh (new pick on each reload), or On view change (new pick when switching between bookmarks, config, inbox, health, or dashboard pages). With auto dark mode, only matching light or dark variants are eligible. While random is on, a Currently showing hint names the active theme.
config.overviewNewFeatureRandomThemeEnable: Open Config → Appearance → Theme and set Random theme to the mode you want.

config.helpFindersBody:
Finders are search shortcuts that send a query straight to an external site instead of searching your bookmarks. ?g nextdash searches Google for “nextdash”; ?w might go to Wikipedia. Open finder mode with ? or from the toolbar, and a fresh install starts with DuckDuckGo on du.

The point is the round trip you skip: no loading the site, finding its search box, then typing. One prefix and your text goes where it was always going.

Defining your own under Pages & tags → Finders takes three things: a shortcut, a display name, and a URL with %s where the query belongs. To get the URL, run any search on the site and copy the address, then replace what you searched for with %s:

  • Wikipedia — https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%s
  • GitHub — https://github.com/search?q=%s
  • Your own docs, an internal wiki, a ticket tracker — anything with a search URL works, including sites only reachable on your own network.

Multi-word queries are encoded for you, so ?w keyboard layout behaves as typing it into the site itself would. Leave the query off entirely — just ?w — and you land on the site’s own search page.

Names and shortcuts have to be unique. Two finders answering to ?g would leave which one runs down to chance, so a duplicate is refused as you type it rather than accepted and quietly ignored later.

Tags can be attached to a finder, which keeps a long list navigable once you have more than a handful. nextDash also counts how often each is used, so the ones you actually reach for rise to the top of the list.

Blending them into ordinary search. Turn on Include finders in search under Behavior → Search & inbox and finders appear alongside bookmarks in normal > results — so one keystroke can reach either, without deciding up front whether you are looking for something you saved or something you want to look up.
config.helpCommandsBody:
: opens the command palette — actions rather than destinations. A lone : lists everything grouped by area, with the commands you use most floating to the top, so the palette gets shorter as it learns what you reach for. Type to narrow, Enter to run.

Many commands take an argument and complete as you type, so you rarely have to remember exact wording — :op is enough to be offered the :open … family.

Opening several at once. These open real browser tabs, so a large selection opens a lot of them:

  • :open last 5 — reopen what you opened most recently. 3, 5 and 10 are offered; any number works.
  • :open tag work · :open category news — everything carrying a tag, or in a category
  • :open pinned — every pinned bookmark
  • :open all — everything on the current page. Worth a glance at the count first.

Finding and filtering without leaving the palette:

  • :tag work — list bookmarks with a tag in the palette, dashboard untouched
  • :filter / :filter clear — apply or drop a dashboard tag filter
  • :find / :find clear — the same for a text filter
  • :recent · :saved · :history — what you opened lately, and what you kept
  • :duplicates · :stale 30 — the two cleanup lists, without opening health

Changing how it looks, which is quicker than opening config and easy to undo:

  • :theme · :dark — switch theme or force dark
  • :layout modern · :density compact · :columns 4 — try a look without committing to it
  • :sort — change the sort mode of the focused category
  • :preview · :animations · :opacity — toggle the smaller visual settings

Housekeeping and getting somewhere:

  • :favicons fetch — re-download every bookmark’s icon
  • :backup · :export — open backups, or download an export straight away
  • :health refresh · :health broken — re-check availability, or jump to what is broken
  • :inbox · :inbox triage — open the inbox, or start working through it
  • :page new · :category new — create one without a trip to config
  • :goto config · :goto health · :goto stats — jump straight to a view
  • :note — edit a bookmark’s note in place
  • :cheat · :help · :whatsnew — the cheat sheet, this guide, or the release notes

The palette is the fastest way to reach anything you do occasionally, but not often enough to remember where it lives.

config.bookmarksPageFilterPromoBody: Pick a page to see only its bookmarks and categories. The address bar becomes a link you can share (#config/bookmarks/…).
config.overviewNewFeatureKeyboardWhat: Move through every config section, sub-tab, and list from the keyboard — no mouse required.
config.overviewNewFeatureKeyboardHow: Use j/k or arrow keys on the section rail, [ and ] for sub-tabs, and list keys on Pages & tags and Bookmarks. Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+K opens Find settings.
config.overviewNewFeatureKeyboardEnable: Press ! for the full cheat sheet, or open Help → Config navigation.
config.overviewNewFeatureFindSettingsWhat: Jump straight to any config section, sub-tab, help topic, or field you have visited.
config.overviewNewFeatureFindSettingsHow: Press Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+K anywhere in config, or click Find settings below Help in the left nav. Type to filter, then Enter to go.
config.overviewNewFeatureFindSettingsEnable: The shortcut works on every config section; the nav button is always below Help.
config.overviewNewFeatureBookmarkPagesWhat: Each page keeps its own category list. The Bookmarks filter shows only categories for the page you pick.
config.overviewNewFeatureBookmarkPagesHow: Choose a page in the filter dropdown to scope categories and deep-link with #config/bookmarks/<pageId>. With All pages, categories show as Page · Category.
config.overviewNewFeatureBookmarkPagesEnable: Open Config → Bookmarks and use the page filter at the top of the list.
config.appearanceDisplayQuickNote: Everyday bookmark row options. Toolbar and tab visibility live on their own tab.
config.helpPageTipsIntro: On the dashboard, a single shortcut hint can rotate above the footer when you enable Show tips above buttons under General → Dashboard (off by default, or turn on with :tips on). The full catalogue lives here if you want to read ahead — collapsed by default so the help page stays scannable.
config.helpPageQuickStartBody:
If you only have half a minute, start here. Open search with >, type part of a bookmark name, and press Enter to open it. Press + or Shift+B when you want the full new-bookmark form, or & on the dashboard for a one-line quick add (name | url | shortcut). Recent bookmarks are always one key away with *, and the keyboard cheat sheet is under ! or F1.

Most layout and behaviour lives under config → General. On desktop, Ctrl+Shift+K finds any setting or help section, while Ctrl+K runs quick actions such as adding a page or refreshing favicons. The ℹ buttons beside individual settings explain what each toggle does without leaving the form.
config.helpPageOnboardingBody:
The first time you open nextDash, a short onboarding wizard helps you pick language, how links open, whether you want date and weather in the header, how search should feel, and how bookmarks respond to keyboard and mouse. You can switch language while the wizard is open, skip any step, or finish later — nothing is locked in until you save in config.

When you start with an empty library, the last steps invite you to create pages and add a first bookmark so the dashboard is useful immediately. After onboarding you may see a one-time What's new summary or a few gentle spotlights (paste URL, preview cards, layout versions). Those are optional nudges, not extra wizards.
config.helpPageConfigGeneralBody:
General is the control room for the whole dashboard. The toolbar at the top of the tab switches between Essentials (everyday choices), Advanced (fine-grained power settings), and All sections (everything on one scrollable page). Essentials covers language, theme, fonts, layout, bookmark display, smart collections, and which footer buttons appear. Advanced adds background tuning, status monitoring, branding, search behaviour, and system tools grouped into cards you can expand or collapse.

Within the bookmark card, display options (icons, shortcuts, badges, link preview) sit above a divider, with behaviour options (sorting, tabs, page names) below — so you can see at a glance what changes how tiles look versus how they act. Tours and onboarding resets live under Advanced → System in a collapsible block if you want to replay a guided tour.

Changes in General do not apply until you press Save. When you do, the dashboard refreshes in place without a full page reload, so you can tweak, save, and immediately see the result.
config.helpPageConfigTabsBody:
Config tabs are grouped so related work stays together. On desktop you will see System (General, Theme, Backups, Stats, Keyboard), Dashboard (Pages, Categories, Bookmarks), Extras (Tags, Finders, Collections), and Help. Group labels sit above the tabs; the active group is highlighted so you always know which area you are in.

When a tab in a group has unsaved changes, a dot appears on the group label — for example System ● while General is dirty. The breadcrumb under the tabs shows a compact path such as General › Layout. The save row at the top tells you whether the current tab needs an explicit save or auto-saves (Collections and Finders save on their own).

On a phone, the tab bar collapses into a simpler set; wide tablets keep the desktop grouping. Keyboard shortcut reference lives in Help → Keyboard shortcuts and in the Keyboard tab under System.
config.helpPageNavigationBody:
nextDash is built for keyboard-first browsing once you learn a handful of keys. Number keys 1–9 jump to pages (when search is closed) and select the first visible bookmark on the new page. Press , for a page overview with counts, navigate with arrows, and confirm with Enter. Move between pages with Shift+← / Shift+→ — plain arrow keys move within the bookmark grid, not across pages.

Start grid navigation with Tab, a click, G followed by a digit, or the first arrow key; then ↑/↓ and ←/→ move the highlight. Enter or Space opens the selected bookmark; Esc clears selection or cancels an unsaved drag reorder. On Mac, Cmd+C copies the highlighted URL. Collapsed categories and items hidden by search are skipped automatically so the highlight never lands on invisible rows.
config.helpPageMobileBody:
On narrow screens, portrait tablets, or touch-first devices, nextDash switches to a lighter chrome so the essentials stay reachable. A short banner on dashboard and config explains what changed; you can dismiss it once you know the layout.

On phones the dashboard footer keeps Search and + Bookmark; commands and finders live inside the search overlay via the >, :, and ? tabs. Recent bookmarks are available through command mode (:open recent or * with a hardware keyboard). The cheat sheet and some footer buttons are desktop-only. Config on a phone focuses on the settings you are most likely to need on the go; the full split-view bookmark editor expects a wider window.
config.helpPageBookmarksDashboardBody:
On the dashboard, bookmarks behave like a small spreadsheet: arrow keys move the selection, ; opens inline edit on the highlighted row, and long-press on the row (not the left drag strip) opens the same editor with touch. The narrow left strip is only for dragging — reorder inside a category or drop into another column.

While inline edit is open, grid navigation pauses so you do not accidentally jump away. Hovering a bookmark can load a rich preview when link preview is enabled in General. Edits to smart-collection rows update the real bookmark everywhere it appears, so tags and notes stay consistent.
config.helpPageSearchBody:
Search is really three modes behind one overlay: > for normal search, : for commands, and ? for finders. Typing : alone opens grouped commands (bookmarks, navigation, layout, smart collections, settings); recent commands float to the top when you reopen it. Filters such as tag:work, category:news, status:online, and page:2 narrow results without changing the dashboard layout.

On desktop, / opens the tag word cloud when that button is enabled; otherwise it follows your fuzzy search setting. Commands like :layout, :density, and :tips on change the UI in place. Turn on Keep search open when empty if you hop in and out of search all day.
config.helpPageDateWeatherBody:
The header can show date, time, and optional weather as a quiet clock line above your bookmarks. Date and time can be toggled independently, with formats ranging from compact numeric styles to weekday-only or long weekday labels. Time supports 24-hour or 12-hour clocks.

When weather is enabled, choose browser geolocation or a manual city, pick Celsius or Fahrenheit, and set how often forecasts refresh. A small icon reflects the current condition. If weather does not appear, check that a location is set and save once — the line renders below date/time when both are active.
config.helpPageSmartBody:
Smart collections are automatic groups such as Today, Recently opened, Stale bookmarks, and Most used. Each can be turned on or off per page and limited to a maximum number of items (use 0 for unlimited). They appear alongside ordinary categories and can be collapsed like any other section.

Enable Tag collections under General → Smart Collections to spawn one dynamic group per tag, with an optional minimum bookmark count so rare tags do not clutter the dashboard.
config.helpPageTagsBody:
Tags are free-form labels you add in config or inline on the dashboard. They are normalised on save (trimmed, lowercased, deduplicated). In search, tag:work filters overlay results without rearranging the grid. On desktop, the tag cloud (/ or the FAB) lets you toggle multiple tags while the modal stays open; matching bookmarks need any selected tag.

Tag collections turn heavily used tags into first-class dashboard sections. Command mode :tag work lists matching bookmarks in the palette only, which is useful when you want a quick list without changing the home view.
config.helpPageCollectionsBody:
Custom collections are rule-based groups you define under Config → Collections. Each has a name, optional emoji icon, match logic (AND or OR), and one or more rules on tag, category, or shortcut. Matching bookmarks appear as read-only sections on the dashboard, sorted with smart collections before ordinary categories.

Collections save immediately — no main Save button required. An optional guided tour walks through creating a demo collection, previewing it on the dashboard, and cleaning up afterward; replay it from System & tools if you want a refresher.
config.helpPageSortingBody:
Pinned bookmarks always float to the top of their category and sort alphabetically among themselves; everyone else follows the category sort mode (manual drag, A–Z, or recent). Click A–Z or Rec in a category header to switch modes; drag handles hide while automatic sort is active.

Categories can be collapsed and renamed with a long press on the header (avoid the sort buttons). Drag the ⠿ grip on a category title to reorder categories on the dashboard; the same order can be edited in config → Categories with drag or arrow keys. Command palette :sort applies to the focused category when you prefer keyboard control.
config.helpPageManageBody:
The config workspace is where pages, categories, and bookmarks are edited in bulk. The Bookmarks tab uses a split view: a filterable list on the left and a detail editor on the right, with an optional Context panel to switch page and category without leaving the tab. Desktop users can press Ctrl+Shift+K to jump to any setting and Ctrl+K for quick actions.

Each bookmark supports name, URL, page, category, shortcut, icon, tags, notes, pin state, and optional status checks. Bulk select supports move, pin toggle, delete, and favicon refresh. Conflict highlighting warns about duplicate URLs or shortcuts before you save. Guided tours for Pages, Categories, Bookmarks, Stats, and Finders replay from Advanced → System when you want a walkthrough again.
config.helpPageStatusBody: Status monitoring optionally pings bookmarks to show online/offline state. Enable it under General → Advanced → Status, choose whether to show ping detail and a loading spinner, and use Skip fast ping check if background noise is too high. For deeper triage, open the Health view in the dashboard to repair broken links, refresh titles, or archive stale entries.
config.helpPageHealthBody:
Health is a dedicated triage view inside the dashboard. Summary cards show totals for healthy, broken, duplicate, stale, and unchecked bookmarks; click a card to filter the list. Search, status filters, and row actions stay in one focused layout.

Each row exposes favicon refresh, health score, and repair actions such as re-check status, detect redirect, refresh title, or archive. Keyboard j/k or arrows move focus; O opens the URL; Enter jumps to the bookmark in config. Layout and theme follow your dashboard settings so the view feels familiar.
config.helpPageBackupBody:
Backups live under Config → Backups. A ZIP export includes pages, bookmarks, categories, finders, settings, and themes — import replaces everything, so export first. From the dashboard, :backup opens the backups tab and :export downloads immediately.

You can also import browser HTML exports (folders become categories; duplicate URLs are skipped) or export all bookmarks to CSV for spreadsheets. A preview before browser import shows how many pages and bookmarks will arrive.
config.helpPageBrandingBody:
Appearance starts under Essentials → Layout: pick Classic or Modern (same structure, different polish), then density, columns, and dashboard title. Advanced → Appearance handles background images, UI font (including an uploaded custom font), and favicon harmonisation. Auto dark mode follows the system theme.

Theme colours are edited on the Theme tab with live preview, packaged palettes, JSON import/export, and per-session undo. Custom favicons upload under Advanced → Branding. Switch layout version from the dashboard with :layoutversion if you want to experiment before saving.
config.helpPageDataBody:
Server data lives in ./data by default (override with NEXTDASH_DATA_DIR for Docker volumes or multiple instances). Open dashboard tabs poll a revision endpoint so bookmark grids refresh when another tab saves changes.

Device-specific settings can be stored in browser local storage when enabled, which lets one computer keep different visual preferences than another. Link preview metadata is cached on the server and flushed periodically to keep hover cards snappy.
config.helpPageExtensionBody:
The browser extension in the extension/ folder saves the current tab to nextDash. Install it unpacked in Chrome, set the server URL, and paste the write token if your server uses NEXTDASH_WRITE_TOKEN. The save form supports optional shortcut (auto-suggested from the title), tags, and notes, with duplicate URL warnings before you commit.

If CORS is restricted, add your chrome-extension:// origin to NEXTDASH_CORS_ORIGINS. After a successful save you can jump straight into nextDash; an open dashboard on the same host may toast and refresh automatically.
config.helpPageSecurityBody:
nextDash has no built-in user accounts — anyone who can reach the URL can read and write data unless you protect it with a VPN, private network, or reverse-proxy authentication. Do not expose plain HTTP to the public internet.

Set NEXTDASH_WRITE_TOKEN so write APIs require the X-NextDash-Token header (pages inject it for same-origin use). Restrict CORS with NEXTDASH_CORS_ORIGINS when using the extension. Outbound fetches validate public IPs to reduce SSRF risk; tune rate limits and activity logging with the environment variables documented in the README security section.
config.helpPageTroubleshootBody:
If bookmarks disappear, check the page selector and category filter in config — an empty page looks like data loss but is usually a filter. Sorting surprises usually mean a category is in A–Z or Recent mode instead of manual order, or pins are doing their job. When tips never show, enable Show tips above buttons under General → Dashboard.

Search gaps often clear up with fuzzy mode or filters like tag:work. Collections that never appear need at least one rule with a value; tag collections need enough tagged bookmarks to meet the minimum. Extension save failures almost always trace to server URL, write token, or CORS. API 401 means a missing token; 429 means rate limits — wait or raise the configured limits.

config.overviewNewFeatureThemePreviewTitle: Try a theme on before you keep it
config.overviewNewFeatureThemePreviewWhat: Finding out what a theme looked like meant switching to it, then switching back if you did not like it — and doing that again for the next one.
config.overviewNewFeatureThemePreviewHow: Open the Theme list under Appearance and move through it: the dashboard behind takes on each theme as you go. Press Esc or click away and you are back where you started. There are 23 new themes to look through as well.
config.overviewNewFeatureThemePreviewEnable: Nothing to switch on. Your choice is only saved once you pick one.
config.overviewNewFeatureServerLogTitle: Read the server log without leaving nextDash
config.overviewNewFeatureServerLogWhat: When something went wrong there was nothing to look at. Finding out why an import failed or a link check never ran meant reaching the machine nextDash runs on.
config.overviewNewFeatureServerLogHow: Data & backups › Server log lists what the server has been doing, keeps itself up to date every few seconds if you want, and colours warnings and errors so they are easy to spot. Search looks through everything kept.
config.overviewNewFeatureServerLogEnable: Nothing to switch on. Limit it by age or by number of entries, and clear the whole lot whenever you like.
config.overviewNewFeatureSettingsSearchTitle: Search finds every setting, not just the ones you have seen
config.overviewNewFeatureSettingsSearchWhat: Looking for “webhook” found nothing at all unless you happened to have opened that tab before, which is the opposite of what a search is for.
config.overviewNewFeatureSettingsSearchHow: Every setting is searchable the moment you open Config, and settings answer to more than their exact label — “uptime”, “wallpaper” and “hotkey” each find the right one even though those words are nowhere on screen.
config.overviewNewFeatureSettingsSearchEnable: Nothing to switch on. Press Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + K anywhere in Config, or use Find settings under the section list.
config.overviewNewFeatureChangedSettingsTitle: See what you have changed from the standard
config.overviewNewFeatureChangedSettingsWhat: Working out why your dashboard behaves differently from the guide meant opening every tab and looking for a ↺ beside each setting.
config.overviewNewFeatureChangedSettingsHow: At a glance now says how many settings differ from the standard and takes you to them. Each tab of settings gained Only changed, and each group a Reset panel that puts the whole lot back at once.
config.overviewNewFeatureChangedSettingsEnable: Nothing to switch on. The line stays out of the way while everything is still standard.
config.overviewNewFeatureToolbarGroupsTitle: Toolbar & tabs is three groups, not one long list
config.overviewNewFeatureToolbarGroupsWhat: Thirteen near-identical “Show the … button” tick boxes in a row, with no way to tell which meant the strip at the top and which the bar at the bottom.
config.overviewNewFeatureToolbarGroupsHow: They are split into the header and the two halves of the button bar, so the group a setting sits in tells you where to look for it on screen. Each group has Show all and Hide all with a count of what is showing.
config.overviewNewFeatureToolbarGroupsEnable: Nothing to switch on — the settings themselves are unchanged, only how they are arranged.
config.overviewNewFeatureInboxExplainTitle: The inbox explains itself, and its numbers add up
config.overviewNewFeatureInboxExplainWhat: A snoozed link is hidden from the list but was still counted above it, so a tile reading 12 could open a list of 9 with nothing explaining the gap.
config.overviewNewFeatureInboxExplainHow: Every count now means what you can act on right now, every pill carries its own, and a sentence under the toolbar says what the active filter selects. The ℹ beside Triage covers snoozing, promoting and the rest.
config.overviewNewFeatureInboxExplainEnable: Nothing to switch on. An empty list now says which kind of empty it is, and long inboxes load as you scroll rather than a page per click.
config.overviewNewFeatureHealthStatsTitle: See how the whole collection is doing
config.overviewNewFeatureHealthStatsWhat: The health view could describe one bookmark in detail and the whole set barely at all: twenty monitors meant twenty heartbeats and no answer to how the week went.
config.overviewNewFeatureHealthStatsHow: The Monitored filter now opens with pooled uptime across every monitor, the least available ones, anything slower than last week, and every outage. The header draws the share of healthy bookmarks over the last 90 days.
config.overviewNewFeatureHealthStatsEnable: Nothing to switch on, though the panel needs something monitored to describe. The trend line starts once you have opened the health view on two separate days.

colors.palettesInfoMessage:
Three ways to edit colors on this tab:

• Dark and Light — change the fallback palettes for the classic dark/light themes in General → Appearance.

• Custom themes — create your own single-palette themes with Add Custom Theme. Each custom theme is one fixed look, not a day/night pair.

• Built-in named themes (Cherry Graphite, Nordic Frost, etc.) are picked in General → Appearance. Their packaged colors live in the server defaults unless you override palettes here.
colors.saveColorsInfoMessage:
Two separate save actions:

• Save colors (this tab) — writes palette edits from the Theme tab to the server. Use this after changing hex values or adding/removing custom themes.

• Save (config header) — stores General settings: which theme is active, layout, bookmarks, language, etc. It does not save color hex values from this tab.

Typical flow: edit colors → Save colors → pick the theme under General → Appearance → Save in the header.
colors.customThemesInfoMessage:
Custom themes are single palettes you create here.

• Add Custom Theme clones the default starter colors. Rename the theme and adjust colors in the editor on the right.

• To use it on the dashboard, select it under General → Appearance and click Save in the config header.

• Auto dark mode (General → Appearance) only works with built-in themes that have separate dark and light variants. It is disabled while a custom theme is selected — custom themes do not switch with your system appearance.

featureTour.step1Body: Discover the most powerful features in a few clicks. You can always skip the tour or restart it later via Config.
featureTour.step2Body: Press ":" or click this button. Change theme with :theme dark, adjust columns with :columns 4, or add a bookmark with :new. Commands are grouped and searchable.
featureTour.step3Body: Press "?" to open your finders. Finders are shortcuts to search engines. A DuckDuckGo finder is ready by default — type "?du linux" to search directly. Add or remove your own finders via Config → Finders.
featureTour.step4Body: Press ">" or click the search button. Use filters like status:online, category:work or tag:dev. Your search history and saved searches are always available.
featureTour.step5Body: Set the number of columns that fits your screen. Favicons are the website icons next to each bookmark — handy for quick recognition.
featureTour.step5ShowIconsHint: Website icons next to each bookmark for quick recognition.
featureTour.step6Body: nextDash automatically groups your bookmarks into dynamic sections. The Today collection shows bookmarks fitting your time of day: work tools in the morning, relaxation in the evening.
featureTour.step6TodayHint: Shows bookmarks that fit your time of day.
featureTour.step6MostUsedHint: Shows your most opened bookmarks in one overview.
featureTour.step7Body: Use arrow keys to navigate, Enter to open and ; to edit inline. Drag via the narrow handle strip on the left to reorder. In Config → Bookmarks you manage everything in bulk, import and export.
featureTour.step8Body: The tour is complete. All features are fully configurable via Config: themes, layout version (Classic or Modern), layout presets, finders, smart collections and bookmark management.
